articles.author: fofo
articles.description: Pagination is not a UI trick, it’s an application-level concern. In Part 9, we implement real pagination in a .NET 10 Clean Architecture application using EF Core, reusable paging contracts, and a paginated Orders API consumed consistently across layers.
articles.title: Creating a .NET 10 Application with Clean Architecture: A Practical Multi-Part Guide – Part 9

articles.author: fofo
articles.description: In Part 8 we add a dedicated ASP.NET Core MVC WebApp that consumes our Clean Architecture API. We introduce typed HttpClients, Razor Views, pagination UI, and optimistic concurrency handling, demonstrating how a real client interacts with the API without violating architectural boundaries or leaking persistence concerns.
articles.title: Creating a .NET 10 Application with Clean Architecture: A Practical Multi-Part Guide – Part 8

articles.author: fofo
articles.description: Part 7 upgrades our Clean Architecture sample with production-grade patterns: FluentValidation for consistent input validation, explicit EF Core transactions for atomic writes, optimistic concurrency using RowVersion, and reliable domain-event publishing via the Outbox pattern. These additions make the system safer under real traffic and failure scenarios, without sacrificing architecture boundaries.
articles.title: Creating a .NET 10 Application with Clean Architecture: A Practical Multi-Part Guide – Part 7

articles.author: fofo
articles.description: Part 6 adds a real-world read endpoint: fetching a customer’s orders with pagination and sorting. We implement a query use case in the Application layer, a fast EF Core 10 projection in Infrastructure, and expose GET /customers/{id}/orders through Swagger. The result is a scalable, Clean Architecture-friendly read model.
articles.title: Creating a .NET 10 Application with Clean Architecture: A Practical Multi-Part Guide – Part 6

articles.author: fofo
articles.description: Part 5 expands our Clean Architecture sample by introducing Orders and OrderItems. We model the domain properly, map relationships with EF Core 10, and implement a CreateOrder use case without leaking persistence into the core. Finally, we expose POST /orders in the API and test everything through Swagger.
articles.title: Creating a .NET 10 Application with Clean Architecture: A Practical Multi-Part Guide – Part 5

articles.author: fofo
articles.description: In Part 4, we replace the in-memory persistence from Part 3 with a real SQL Server database using EF Core 10. We introduce a DbContext, implement repository interfaces, wire dependency injection, and create migrations, without changing domain logic or API endpoints, demonstrating the practical value of Clean Architecture.
articles.title: Creating a .NET 10 Application with Clean Architecture: A Practical Multi-Part Guide – Part 4

articles.author: fofo
articles.description: In Part 3, we move from setup to real code. We design the first domain entity, implement the CreateCustomer use case in the Application layer, and expose a /customers endpoint through the API. With Swagger enabled, we can already test a complete vertical slicewithout using a database yet.
articles.title: Creating a .NET 10 Application with Clean Architecture: A Practical Multi-Part Guide – Part 3

articles.author: fofo
articles.description: In Part 2, we prepare the foundation of our application using Visual Studio 2026. We create the solution and projects, wire the correct Clean Architecture dependencies, install required packages, and configure Swagger so the API runs and opens automatically, before writing any real business logic.
articles.title: Creating a .NET 10 Application with Clean Architecture: A Practical Multi-Part Guide – Part 2

articles.author: fofo
articles.description: Clean Architecture is a way to structure a .NET solution so that your business logic doesn’t get held hostage by frameworks, databases, UI choices, or whatever trendy library shows up next year.
articles.title: Creating a .NET 10 Application with Clean Architecture: A Practical Multi-Part Guide – Part 1

articles.description:
In the world of quantum computing, generating true randomness is one of the most fundamental applications. But how do we know that a sequence of numbers is truly random and generated by a quantum process, rather than by a classical simulation or a pre-determined list?
In this post, we will explore a protocol to generate high-quality random numbers using a quantum computer, based on the recent paper Certified randomness amplification by dynamically probing remote random quantum states (Liu et al, arXiv:2511.03686, 2025). We will implement the core of this protocol using Q# for the quantum kernel and Python for the orchestration and verification, and then run it on a Q# simulator.
articles.title: Certified Randomness Amplification with Q#

articles.description:
If you visited this blog before, chances are you are familiar with Q# Bridge, a library that I have been working on for quite a while, that allows you to run Q# quantum simulations and access a number of Q# compiler/QDK features from multiple popular high-level languages such as C#, Swift, Python and Kotlin.
Today, I would like to shortly talk about a brand new feature in the library - the ability to generate Quantikz LaTeX circuits from Q# source code.
articles.title: Generating Quantikz LaTeX Circuits from Q# Code

articles.description:
I’ve recently been working on setting up a bunch of Agent Framework samples, which would showcase the cooperation between cloud agents (backed by LLMs in the cloud) and local agents (running on your own machine). Since I primarily work on a Mac, the natural choice for me was to use MLX as the local model runner, which required a bit of bootstrapping - and felt quite tedious. So, the natural next step was to create a library that would make it easy to integrate MLX models into Agent Framework applications, since there wasn’t one available yet.
Today, I’m excited to announce the release of the MLX Integration Library for Agent Framework! This library simplifies the process of integrating MLX models into your Agent Framework applications, allowing you to leverage local Mac AI capabilities seamlessly alongside cloud-based agents.
articles.title: Introducing the MLX Integration Library for Agent Framework
